items.title: Reactivity of the pi bond (printed as a second 11.7.1)

source_refs.note: Reactivity of the pi bond, printed as a second 11.7.1 on pages 257-258, with the Did You Know and Interesting Information boxes.

blocks.text: Alkenes are more reactive than alkanes because of the double bond. In the pi bond the probability of finding the electrons is away from the line joining the two nuclei, so the pi electrons are less firmly held between the nuclei; a pi bond is therefore weak compared with a sigma bond and breaks comparatively easily during a reaction, making alkenes a reactive group of compounds. Moreover, the loosely held pi electrons are more exposed to attack by electrophilic reagents, so alkenes undergo electrophilic addition reactions very easily.

blocks.title: Electrophile and nucleophile
blocks.text: An electrophile is a species that can act as an electron-pair acceptor, represented by E+. A nucleophile is a species that can act as a donor of a pair of electrons, represented by Nu-. Alkenes act as nucleophiles because they contain pi electrons.
Plants produce ethene as a natural ripening hormone; fruits and vegetables are often picked unripe for efficient harvesting and transport and exposed to ethene so that they ripen in a short time.

blocks.alt: Top left: ethene drawn flat with a sigma bond between the carbons and two pink lobes above and below for the pi bond, with notes on sp2 hybridisation. Top middle: the carbocation series methyl, primary, secondary, tertiary with an arrow of increasing stability and notes on the inductive effect. Top right: the two preparations of ethene. Bottom: the mechanisms of bromine with ethene and of hydrogen bromide with ethene and with propene, with Markovnikov's rule.
blocks.caption: The ethene double bond, carbocation stability and the inductive effect, preparation of ethene, and electrophilic addition mechanisms (original diagram after Figures 11.8 to 11.17 and topics 11.6.2 to 11.8.1).
blocks.long_description: The double bond of ethene is a sigma bond between sp2 carbons plus a pi bond from the sideways overlap of p orbitals, which keeps the molecule flat and leaves the pi electrons loosely held and exposed. Those electrons attack an electrophile such as the positive end of a polarised bromine molecule or the hydrogen of hydrogen bromide, giving a carbocation that a nucleophile then completes. Carbocations are stabilised by electron-pushing alkyl groups, so tertiary is more stable than secondary than primary, and with propene the hydrogen adds to the carbon that already has more hydrogens to form the secondary carbocation, which is Markovnikov's rule. Ethene itself is made by eliminating water from ethanol with hot concentrated sulfuric acid or hydrogen bromide from bromoethane with alcoholic potassium hydroxide.

blocks.prompt: Which of H2, H+ and OH- is likely to act as a nucleophile and which as an electrophile, and why (Quick Check 11.5b to e)?
blocks.explanation: OH- is the nucleophile: it carries a negative charge and lone pairs it can donate. H+ is the electrophile: it has no electrons and accepts a pair. H2 is neither; it is a non-polar molecule with a filled sigma bond and no charge or lone pair to offer or accept.

items: Pi electrons lie away from the internuclear line, are weakly held and exposed: the pi bond breaks easily and attracts electrophiles, so alkenes undergo electrophilic addition.
Electrophile E+ = electron-pair acceptor; nucleophile Nu- = electron-pair donor; the alkene's pi electrons make it a nucleophile. Ethene is a plant ripening hormone.
